chapter_theme: Under the heading கல்லாதார், six verses on the unlearned and the learned in company: the unlearned man's right judgements are luck, his insights falter when spoken before the learned and count for nothing unspoken, and the learned man who speaks among the unlearned turns his good words bad and lapses in conduct; the unlearned who challenge the learned want what they cannot do.

11.reading: Those who have neither learnt for themselves nor heard from the mouths of the learned do not understand things clearly, and if such a man ever lights on the truth it is no more his doing than a fruit picked up under the naaval tree.
11.nuance: The verse names two routes to knowledge, one's own study and listening to the learned, and denies the man who has taken neither; the proverb then grants that he may be right on occasion and takes the credit from him, since the fruit fell and was not earned. As printed, line 1 reads சுற்றானும் சுற்றார்வாய், which makes poor sense under the heading; the reading assumes கற்றானும் கற்றார்வாய்.

pazhamozhi.literal: a fruit got under the naaval (jamun) tree

story.act: no story; the proverb stands for any windfall that drops to whoever happens to stand below

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an unlearned man's occasional true judgement is luck, not knowledge

12.reading: When an unlearned man voices before the learned some very fine point he has hit upon, it falters, because, as the saying goes, no answer comes without a question going before it, and no deed without a dream going before it.
12.nuance: Only the first half of the paired proverb does the work: among the learned every statement is met by questions, and the unlearned man's insight, never tested by questioning, gives way under them. The second half (the dream before the deed) rides along as the proverb's usual partner. The verse is addressed to a woman (நல்லாய்!); the address is a frame, not the counsel's audience. Its first line is shared, nearly word for word, with verse 13.

pazhamozhi.proverb: வினாமுந் துறாத உரையில்லை; இல்லை கனாமுந் துறாத வினை
pazhamozhi.literal: there is no answer that a question does not precede, and no deed that a dream does not precede

story.act: no story; the proverb states a general order of things, question before answer and omen before act

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the unlearned man's insight collapses when the learned question it

13.reading: Since the very fine point an unlearned man has found is hard for him to show, there is no sense in his rating himself highly as one of the good, for even those able to bend others by speech have said nothing if they do not speak.
13.nuance: Read with 12, the verse closes the unlearned man's last exit: spoken before the learned his insight falters (12), and kept unspoken it does not exist for anyone (13). Line 3 is obscure: the printed வெகுண்(டு)அரு கிற்பார்க்கும் carries an editor's bracket and its sense, perhaps those who can overawe or come at others in anger, is not certain; the reading takes the line only as 'even the powerful in speech'.

pazhamozhi.literal: if one does not speak, nothing is said

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the able speaker who stays silent, and through him to the unlearned man whose insight cannot be shown

pazhamozhi.applied_to: insight that cannot be put into words earns no standing

14.reading: The deep subtleties that learning yields, spoken before the unlearned, turn every good thing said into a bad one, lord of the land of high hills, just as for those who have no kin even a city is like a forest.
14.nuance: The image makes the audience a kind of kin: the learned man among the unlearned is as friendless as a stranger in a crowded city, and what is good in his words finds no one to receive it, so it does harm instead. The text has சுழிநுட்பம் here where 12 and 13 have கழிநுட்பம்.

pazhamozhi.literal: to those without their own people even a city is like a forest

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the learned speaker who finds no hearers of his own kind

pazhamozhi.applied_to: learned speech among the unlearned is not merely wasted but turned to harm

15.reading: For a man nothing is worse than making a fine, well-wrought speech among the unlearned, since there is no lowness greater than a lapse of conduct and no height greater than conduct.
15.nuance: The verse classes the choice of audience as conduct: holding forth among the unlearned is an இழுக்கம், a lapse that lowers the speaker, not merely a waste of eloquence. The proverb's ozhukkam and izhukkam pair is the pair of the Kural's chapter on conduct, here used as a known saying.

pazhamozhi.proverb: இழுக்கத்தின் மிக்க இழிவில்லை இல்லை ஒழுக்கத்தின் மிக்க உயர்வு
pazhamozhi.literal: no disgrace exceeds a lapse, no elevation exceeds right conduct

story.act: no story; the proverb is a general maxim on conduct

pazhamozhi.applied_to: speaking learnedly among the unlearned is a lapse that lowers the speaker

16.reading: For the unlearned to provoke those who live by learning, take up a contest of words and rise itching for a fight is like a lame man who cannot even walk wanting to sport with an elephant.
16.nuance: The proverb's point is the gap between the wish and the means: the lame man cannot walk, yet wants a game with the strongest of beasts. பிடிப்பூணி is obscure; it may tie the elephant to a she-elephant (பிடி) or to a fetter, and the reading leaves it as 'an elephant' only. சொற்றாற்று and சுனைத்து are also uncommon; the reading takes them as a fight in words and an itch to rise.

pazhamozhi.literal: a lame man's wish to play with an elephant

story.act: no story; the lame man of the proverb is a type, applied to the unlearned who pick a quarrel with the learned

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the unlearned man's challenge to the learned is a desire far beyond his strength

links.note: Kural 414 offers listening as the help left to one who has not studied; Pazhamozhi 11 names study and listening as the two routes and condemns the man who has taken neither.
links.teaches: Together they show listening as the fallback the Kural concedes and Pazhamozhi makes the minimum, so the man without even that has only luck left.
links.list_adds: it sets study and hearing side by side as two routes and adds a proverb that strips credit from any lucky hit.

links.note: Naladiyar 270 says those with understanding are as the learned though they have not studied; Pazhamozhi 11 says one who has neither studied nor listened does not understand clearly and is right only by chance. The conflict holds on the reading that 270's உணர்வுடையார் need no study or hearing at all.
links.teaches: The pair splits on whether native understanding can stand in for learning: the Naladiyar lets inner sense make a man learned, Pazhamozhi treats an untaught man's right judgement as a windfall.
links.list_adds: its proverb turns the untaught man's success into chance, the very case the quatrain credits to inner understanding.

links.note: Both say the unlearned man's standing falters (சோர்வு படும்) when he speaks; Pazhamozhi 12 places it before the learned and gives the cause through its proverb.
links.teaches: The Kural states the faltering bare and leaves the hearer unnamed; Pazhamozhi supplies the learned hearers and the mechanism, the questions every claim must meet.
links.list_adds: the proverb explains why the speech falters: among the learned every statement must survive a question it has never faced.

links.note: The two verses open with the same line on the unlearned man's fine point; 12 has it falter when spoken, 13 has it count for nothing when unspoken.
links.teaches: Read together they form a dilemma: speaking exposes the unlearned man's insight and silence erases it, so without learning there is no way for it to count.

links.note: Kural 403 calls the unlearned very good if they keep silent before the learned; Pazhamozhi 13 says silence leaves their insight unshown and so gives no ground for thinking themselves good.
links.teaches: The Kural's ironic praise of the silent unlearned is limited by Pazhamozhi: silence spares them shame but cannot make them one of the good.
links.list_adds: its proverb makes silence a nullity, so the goodness the couplet grants the silent unlearned is goodness with nothing in it.

links.note: Naladiyar 254 says the unlearned man among the wise is a dog sitting if silent and a dog barking if he speaks; Pazhamozhi 13 says his unspoken insight is nothing.
links.teaches: Both refuse the unlearned any good way to be present among the learned, the Naladiyar by contempt for his person, Pazhamozhi by an argument that an unshown insight is no insight.
links.list_adds: it argues from the proverb on speech rather than from an insulting image, so the denial rests on how insight is shown, not on what the man is.

links.note: Kural 720 likens holding forth before those not of one's own group to nectar spilled in a dirty yard; Pazhamozhi 14 says learned speech before the unlearned turns good to bad, as a city is a forest to one without kin.
links.teaches: Both measure an audience by kinship (தங்கணத்தார், தமர்), but the Kural's nectar is only wasted while Pazhamozhi's good words become harmful, which makes the wrong audience an active danger.
links.list_adds: its proverb casts the speaker, not the speech, as the one stranded, a man among strangers in a city.

links.note: Naladiyar 255 has the worthy keep their learning unspoken, even when asked, where it will not be taken in; Pazhamozhi 14 gives the cost of speaking there.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar gives the practice, silence even when asked, and Pazhamozhi gives the reason, that good words among the unlearned turn bad.
links.list_adds: it names the outcome the worthy avoid, the reversal of good into bad, which the quatrain leaves implicit.

links.note: Kural 719 says those who speak well in a good assembly should not speak in a mean one, even by slip; Pazhamozhi 15 calls fine speech among the unlearned the worst thing for a man and a lapse of conduct.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi moves the Kural's rule of assembly into the field of ozhukkam, so speaking to the wrong audience is a fault of character that lowers the speaker, not only a tactical error.
links.list_adds: it ranks the act as the worst of things for a man and proves it with the conduct maxim, which the couplet does not invoke.

links.note: Kural 137 says conduct brings high standing and lapses bring blame; Pazhamozhi 15 uses the same ozhukkam and izhukkam pair as a proverb to judge speech among the unlearned.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the Kural's conduct couplet circulating as a proverb and being applied to a case the couplet never names, the choice of whom to speak before.
links.list_adds: it applies the conduct maxim to a particular act, eloquence in the wrong company, and so widens what counts as a lapse.

links.note: Kural 402 likens the unlearned man's desire to speak to a desire for womanhood in one without breasts; Pazhamozhi 16 likens his challenge to the learned to a lame man wanting to play with an elephant.
links.teaches: Both frame the unlearned man's ambition as desire without the faculty, but Pazhamozhi moves it from wanting to speak to picking a fight, where the lame man's wish also courts danger.
links.list_adds: its image adds danger to incapacity, since an elephant can crush the lame man who wants to play.

links.note: Naladiyar 312 has the bad scholar, worsted in assembly, slap his shoulders and rise to fight; Pazhamozhi 16 has the unlearned provoke the learned and rise itching for a contest.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar shows the fight as what follows defeat, Pazhamozhi as what the unlearned man starts; together they mark aggression as the unlearned man's response to learning before and after the contest.
links.list_adds: its proverb judges the challenge hopeless from the start, while the quatrain warns the disciplined to keep away.

source_issues: 11 line 1: சுற்றானும் சுற்றார்வாய் is probably a misprint for கற்றானும் கற்றார்வாய் (learning and hearing from the learned); the reading assumes the correction.
12 and 13 share an almost identical first line (கல்லாதான் கண்ட கழிநுட்பம்), while 14 has சுழிநுட்பம்; either may be a copying variant.
13 line 3: வெகுண்(டு)அரு கிற்பார்க்கும் carries an editorial bracket and its sense is obscure.
16 lines 3-4: the quotation opens at முடவன், leaving தானும் நடவான் outside, though the clause belongs to the proverb's image; the quotation marks may be misplaced. பிடிப்பூணி is obscure.
